title: Deep learning and accelerated workloads
summary: Shapes as contracts, a two-layer network computed by hand, how a loss and its gradient move weights, what embeddings store, what training holds in GPU memory that inference does not, when to fine-tune and when to retrieve, how data parallelism shares gradients, and how to place GPU compute on the platform only after a simpler model has fallen short.
outcomes: Read what each axis of a tensor counts, predict the shape of a matrix product and diagnose a shape mismatch from its error text.
Compute a two-layer forward pass, its log loss and an output-layer gradient by hand, and explain why a switched-off unit receives no update.
Separate training from inference, size a batch against a GPU memory budget, choose fine-tuning or retrieval for a stated need, and explain data parallelism.
Name the documented routes to GPUs on Databricks with their status, and write an accelerated-workload design with unexecuted steps labelled, a CPU smoke test first and a simpler baseline to beat.
startingAssumptions: The machine learning fundamentals module has taught baselines, held-out evaluation and training versus serving at a conceptual level.
Multiplying a row by a column and summing is familiar; no calculus beyond 'the slope of a curve' is assumed.
editorialRationale: Deep learning is usually taught either as magic or as calculus. This module takes one Cinderline reading through a network small enough to compute by hand, with the numbers reproduced by a NumPy run on CPU, so every later idea (gradients, embeddings, batches, memory, data parallelism) is a change to arithmetic the learner has already done. Platform material comes last and is written as verification items with preview and deprecation status, and the module ends by making the network earn its cost against a simpler model, because the most common field mistake is starting a GPU project before a baseline exists.

concepts.definition: The tuple giving how many items each axis of an array holds; the item type (dtype) is stored separately.
concepts.example: A batch of 32 vibration windows of 256 steps and 3 axes has shape (32, 256, 3).

concepts.definition: A product A @ B runs only when A's last axis and B's first axis have the same size, which the result then drops.
concepts.example: (3, 2) @ (2, 2) returns (3, 2); (1, 3) @ (2, 2) raises a core-dimension mismatch.

concepts.definition: A weight-matrix multiplication plus a bias, followed by an activation function, turning one vector of numbers into the next.
concepts.example: Layer 1 maps the reading [0.5, 1.0] to pre-activations [-1.0, 0.25] before ReLU.

concepts.definition: The function max(z, 0), which passes positive values and turns negatives into zero, bending an otherwise linear network.
concepts.example: ReLU turns the pre-activations [-1.0, 0.25] into [0, 0.25].

concepts.definition: The ordered arithmetic that carries an input through every layer to the output, here ending in a sigmoid probability.
concepts.example: The reading [0.5, 1.0] ends at score 0.5 and defect probability 0.6225.

concepts.definition: A number scoring how wrong a prediction is against its label; training tries to make its average small.
concepts.example: Predicting 0.6225 for a real defect gives log loss -ln(0.6225) = 0.4741.

concepts.definition: Repeatedly moving each weight a small step against the gradient of the loss, the step scaled by a learning rate.
concepts.example: W2[1] moves from 4.0 to about 4.0094 at learning rate 0.1.

concepts.definition: A learned lookup table mapping a categorical index to a vector the next layer can multiply, updated by gradients like other weights.
concepts.example: Supplier code S-0331 is index 2 and returns a learned three-number row.

concepts.definition: Training repeats forward, loss, backward and update over labelled batches; inference runs one forward pass with frozen weights.
concepts.example: Scoring 200,000 production clips changes no weight; a new labelled run does.

concepts.definition: The number of examples whose gradients are averaged into one update; it sets steps per epoch and activation memory.
concepts.example: 64,000 windows at batch 64 give 1,000 steps per epoch.

concepts.definition: Accelerator memory holding weights, gradients, optimizer state and one batch's activations during a training step.
concepts.example: 80 MB fixed plus 6 MB per window: batch 512 needs 3,152 MB against 2,048 MB (synthetic).

concepts.definition: Adding gradients from several small batches before one optimizer step, keeping the effective batch while holding one small batch's activations.
concepts.example: Batch 64 accumulated over four steps updates like batch 256 but needs 464 MB (synthetic).

concepts.definition: Continuing to train an existing model on new examples so that its weights, and therefore its habits, change.
concepts.example: Examples of six-field defect codes change how the model formats answers.

concepts.definition: Finding relevant passages at request time and placing them in the model's input, leaving the weights unchanged.
concepts.example: This Monday's bulletin is indexed and cited in answers the same day.

concepts.definition: Every worker keeps a full model copy, processes a different slice of the batch, and averages gradients with the others before each identical update.
concepts.example: Two workers take 128 windows each of a 256 batch and exchange gradients every step.

visuals.caption: Each new axis counts something new; the batch axis comes first and the bytes follow from the product of the sizes. Synthetic teaching example.

What the batch costs: Memory is the product of the sizes times bytes per item. Equation: 32 × 256 × 3 = 24,576 values × 4 bytes (float32) = 98,304 bytes ≈ 98 KB of input

visuals.title: The inner sizes decide whether a product runs
visuals.alt: Four equations: matching inner sizes that vanish, a stacked batch product, a mismatch error, and a product that runs but computes the wrong thing.
visuals.caption: The two inner sizes must agree and disappear; outer axes carry through; a legal product can still be the wrong one.
visuals.textEquivalent:
Inner sizes agree: The 2 of the batch meets the 2 of the weight and disappears. Equation: X (3, 2) @ W (2, 2) → (3, 2): three readings in, three pairs of hidden values out

Leading axes carry through: Batch and time axes are treated as a stack and kept. Equation: (32, 256, 3) @ (3, 8) → (32, 256, 8), as run with NumPy in this build

Inner sizes disagree: The product refuses before any arithmetic and names both sizes. Equation: (1, 3) @ (2, 2) → ValueError: matmul: … core dimension 0 … (size 2 is different from 3)

Legal but wrong: Square weights accept either orientation, so the shape check cannot catch this. Equation: X (3, 2) @ W1 (2, 2) runs but computes W1ᵀx per row; the network needs X @ W1.T

visuals.title: Two linear maps and a bend
visuals.alt: A two-input network: inputs feed two hidden units through ReLU into one output. Without ReLU the two layers collapse into one linear map; with ReLU, unit one switches off for this reading.
visuals.caption: Remove the bend and the second layer adds nothing; keep it and different inputs switch different units off. Hand-chosen weights. Synthetic teaching example.
visuals.textEquivalent:
Two layers with a bend: Each hidden unit is a weighted sum plus a bias, passed through ReLU, then combined by the output layer. Nodes: x1 vibration: 0.5. Standardized input. (context); x2 temperature: 1.0. Standardized input. (context); hidden unit 1: 1.0·x1 − 2.0·x2 + 0.5, then ReLU. (selected); hidden unit 2: 0.5·x1 + 1.0·x2 − 1.0, then ReLU. (selected); output score: 2.0·h1 + 4.0·h2 − 0.5, then sigmoid. (selected). Relationships: x1 vibration → hidden unit 1: ×1.0; x2 temperature → hidden unit 1: ×−2.0; x1 vibration → hidden unit 2: ×0.5; x2 temperature → hidden unit 2: ×1.0; hidden unit 1 → output score: ×2.0; hidden unit 2 → output score: ×4.0.

No bend: one layer in disguise: Without ReLU the two products and biases fold into one weight row and one bias. Equation: W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = (W2W1)x + (W2b1 + b2) = [4.0, 0.0]·x − 3.5 → −1.5 for x = [0.5, 1.0]

With the bend: a unit switches off: ReLU zeroes unit one for this reading, so only unit two reaches the output. Nodes: x1 vibration: 0.5. Standardized input. (context); x2 temperature: 1.0. visuals.title: One reading through the network, by hand
visuals.alt: Four equations carry the reading [0.5, 1.0] through layer 1, ReLU, layer 2 and the sigmoid to 0.6225, then a table shows three readings as one batch.
visuals.caption: Every intermediate value is printed so you can recompute it; the batch reuses the same weights for three readings. Hand-chosen, untrained weights.
visuals.textEquivalent:
Layer 1: linear map: Each hidden unit's weighted sum plus its bias. Equation: z1 = W1x + b1 = [1.0×0.5 − 2.0×1.0 + 0.5, 0.5×0.5 + 1.0×1.0 − 1.0] = [−1.0, 0.25]

Layer 2: the score: The output layer weighs the hidden values and adds its bias. Equation: z2 = W2h + b2 = 2.0×0 + 4.0×0.25 − 0.5 = 0.5

Sigmoid: a probability: The sigmoid squeezes any score into (0, 1). Equation: p = 1 / (1 + e^(−0.5)) = 0.6225, a 62% defect probability

visuals.title: From a wrong-ish answer to a weight update
visuals.alt: Four equations: the log loss of 0.6225 for a real defect, the output gradient, the gradient for each output weight, and one update with learning rate 0.1.
visuals.caption: The error signal reaches only the weight whose unit was on; one small step raises the defect probability slightly. Hand-chosen weights, label y = 1.
visuals.textEquivalent:
Score the prediction: The reading was a real defect; the loss is small only if p is near 1. Equation: loss = −ln(p) = −ln(0.6225) = 0.4741 (label y = 1; a perfect prediction scores 0)

Output gradient: For a sigmoid with log loss the gradient at the score is prediction minus label. Equation: ∂loss/∂z2 = p − y = 0.6225 − 1 = −0.3775 (negative: the score should rise)

Gradients for the output weights: Each weight's gradient is the error times the value that flowed through it. Equation: ∂loss/∂W2 = (p − y) × h = −0.3775 × [0, 0.25] = [−0.0 (a signed zero), −0.0944]

One gradient-descent step: Move against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate. Equation: W2 ← W2 − 0.1 × [−0.0, −0.0944] = [2.0, 4.0094]; p rises from 0.6225 to 0.6230

questions.prompt: Cinderline's vibration batch is stored batch-first with shape (64, 512, 6). A colleague says the batch holds 512 windows. What does each axis count?

options.text: 64 windows, each 512 time steps long, each step carrying 6 channel readings.
options.rationale: Batch-first puts the count of examples on axis 0; 512 is the length of each window and 6 the channels per step.

options.text: 512 windows of 64 time steps, each carrying 6 channels.
options.rationale: This reads the middle axis as the batch; in a batch-first layout the first number counts examples, so 512 is the time axis.

options.text: 6 windows of 64 by 512 readings each.
options.rationale: The last axis is usually the channel count per step; treating it as the batch reverses the layout the model expects.

options.text: 196,608 windows, because a shape multiplies out to the number of examples.
options.rationale: 64 x 512 x 6 = 196,608 is the number of individual values, which sets memory, not the number of examples.

questions.prompt: X holds 8 readings of 5 features, shape (8, 5). Which weight shape lets X @ W run and return (8, 3)?

options.rationale: The inner sizes 5 and 5 agree and disappear, leaving 8 rows of 3 outputs.
The inner sizes are 5 and 3, so the product raises a core-dimension mismatch; this is the transpose, which needs X @ W.T.
Shaped like the desired output, not like a weight; the inner sizes 5 and 8 disagree and the product fails.
Neither inner size matches: X's last axis is 5 and this weight's first axis is 3, so no arithmetic runs.

questions.prompt: With the worked weights (W1 = [[1.0, -2.0], [0.5, 1.0]], b1 = [0.5, -1.0], W2 = [2.0, 4.0], b2 = -0.5), the reading x = [1.0, 0.0] arrives. What does the network produce?

options.rationale: z1 = [1.5, -0.5]; ReLU zeroes the second unit; 2.0 x 1.5 - 0.5 = 2.5; sigmoid(2.5) = 0.9241.
This skips ReLU, so the negative unit subtracts 4.0 x 0.5 from the score; the bend is exactly what removes that.
This forgets the output bias b2 = -0.5; every layer adds its bias after the product.
2.5 is the score before the sigmoid; a probability must lie between 0 and 1, which the sigmoid guarantees.

questions.prompt: In the worked backward step the gradient for W2 came out as [-0., -0.0944]. Why is its first entry zero?

options.text: Hidden unit one output 0 after ReLU for this reading, and W2[0]'s gradient is (p - y) x h[0].
options.rationale: A weight's gradient is scaled by the value flowing through it; h[0] = 0, so the error signal gives W2[0] no instruction.

options.text: The learning rate for W2[0] is zero.
options.rationale: The learning rate scales the step after the gradient is computed and is the same for both weights here; it cannot make a gradient zero.

options.text: W2[0] has already reached its best value.
options.rationale: The zero comes from the input to that weight, not from optimality; for x = [2.0, 0.0] unit one is active and the same weight gets a non-zero gradient.

options.text: The loss for this reading is already zero.
options.rationale: The loss is 0.4741 and the output gradient p - y = -0.3775 is not zero; only the path through unit one is cut.

questions.prompt: The defect model has a 40-row supplier embedding table. A new supplier code, S-0917, appears in production and inference fails with an index error. What is the sound fix for the next training run?

options.text: Reserve an 'unknown' index, map codes unseen in training to it at both training and inference, and retrain so that row is learned.
options.rationale: The table's size is fixed when built; an unknown row gives every new code a trained vector until enough data exists to give it its own.

options.text: Append a random row for S-0917 at inference time.
options.rationale: A random vector was never seen by the layers that follow, so its predictions are arbitrary, and resizing the table changes the model's parameters.

options.text: Feed the supplier code as a raw integer instead.
options.rationale: An integer imposes a false order and distance between suppliers, which is exactly what the learned vector avoided.

options.text: Increase the embedding dimension.
options.rationale: A wider vector adds numbers to each existing row; the missing piece is a row for the new index, which the dictionary size controls.

questions.prompt: A colleague says the defect model 'keeps learning' because it has scored 200,000 production clips since deployment. What has happened to its weights?

options.text: Nothing: inference runs frozen forward passes; weights change only in a training run that computes losses against labels and applies updates.
options.rationale: Serving computes predictions only; there is no loss, gradient or optimizer step without labels and a training loop.

options.text: They drift slightly with every clip scored.
options.rationale: Drift of this kind would need a gradient and an update at request time, and neither exists in inference.

options.text: They are averaged across the clips each night.
options.rationale: No mechanism averages weights over predictions; averaging gradients happens only inside a training step.

options.text: They update whenever a prediction is wrong.
options.rationale: The service cannot know which predictions are wrong: inspection labels arrive later and feed a new, separate training run.

questions.prompt: Synthetic budget: 80 MB fixed for weights, gradients and optimizer state, 6 MB of activations per window, 2,048 MB of GPU memory. Which is the largest of these batch sizes that fits?

options.rationale: 80 + 320 x 6 = 2,000 MB, inside 2,048 MB; the next option up does not fit.
2,048 / 6 = 341 ignores the 80 MB fixed cost; weights, gradients and optimizer state are present at every batch size.
80 + 384 x 6 = 2,384 MB, over the budget; this batch fails with out-of-memory.
256 fits at 1,616 MB, but 320 also fits, so it is not the largest option.

questions.prompt: Cinderline wants its maintenance assistant to answer from this week's bulletins, cite each one, and stay current as bulletins change every Monday. Which approach fits?

options.text: Retrieval: index the bulletins, rebuild the index when they change, place matching passages in the prompt and cite them.
options.rationale: Changing facts that need citations are what retrieval is for; refreshing the index updates answers without touching weights.

options.text: Fine-tune the model every Monday on the new bulletins.
options.rationale: Weekly retuning costs GPU time, still produces no citation, and leaves last week's facts in the weights.

options.text: One continued pre-training run on all past bulletins.
options.rationale: The weights would be frozen at the training date and would miss next Monday's bulletin.

options.text: Raise the serving batch size so more bulletins fit.
options.rationale: Batch size sets how many requests are processed together; it does not change what facts the model sees.

questions.prompt: A training step runs out of GPU memory at batch 64 on one GPU. A colleague proposes data parallelism over four GPUs, still with batch 64 on each. What happens to per-GPU memory?

options.text: It stays about the same: each GPU still holds a full model copy, its gradients, its optimizer state and 64 windows' activations.
options.rationale: Data parallelism splits a global batch across workers; keeping 64 per worker keeps each worker's memory, so the failure remains.

options.text: It falls to a quarter.
options.rationale: It would fall only if each worker's local batch shrank; the model is copied to every worker, not divided among them.

options.text: It disappears because the all-reduce moves activations off the GPU.
options.rationale: The all-reduce exchanges gradients between workers; activations stay on each GPU for its own backward pass.

options.text: The model is split across the four GPUs, so the weights take a quarter each.
options.rationale: Splitting the model is sharded or model parallelism, such as FSDP; data parallelism keeps a full copy on every worker.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague fluent in SQL asks why the network needs ReLU at all: 'two matrix multiplications are already a model.' Explain, using the worked weights, what happens without the bend.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Without ReLU the two layers compose into one: W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = (W2W1)x + (W2b1 + b2). With the worked weights that is [4.0, 0.0] times x minus 3.5, a single linear map, so the second layer added no new shape of decision. With ReLU, unit one is switched off for x = [0.5, 1.0] and on for x = [2.0, 0.0]; different inputs use different units, which lets the network draw boundaries a single weighted sum cannot. It is like a CASE expression between two projections: remove it and the two projections merge into one.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer shows the algebraic collapse with numbers rather than asserting it, and then shows the mechanism ReLU adds. Using sigmoid or tanh as the bend is an acceptable alternative; the point is any nonlinearity.

beats.title: A tensor's shape says what each axis counts
beats.outcome: Read a batch-first shape axis by axis and state what each number counts and what the batch costs in bytes.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-deep-learning-shape-concept|tensor shape]] is a tuple of counts, one per axis; the dtype, such as float32, is stored separately. Notice in the table how one Cinderline reading is (2,), a vibration window adds a time axis to become (256, 3), and a batch puts 32 windows on a new first axis: (32, 256, 3). Read each number as "how many of what". The last state multiplies the sizes: the shape alone fixes how many bytes the batch occupies.
beats.hint: Ask what a single example looks like before asking about the batch.

handbook.markdown:
A tensor is an array with a shape and a dtype. NumPy's reference defines the shape as a tuple of non-negative integers, one per dimension, and keeps the item type as a separate data-type object; PyTorch creates floating-point tensors as float32 by default. The same data can therefore be the same shape in two dtypes with different memory, or the same bytes in two shapes with different meanings.

Three habits make shapes readable:

- **Name every axis.** Write `# (batch, time, channel)` beside every array you create. A comment is cheap; a transposed axis is a silent bug.
- **Batch first.** Most layers expect examples on axis 0. When data arrives time-first from a sensor export, fix it once at load time with `x.transpose(1, 0, 2)` or its equivalent, and assert the result.
- **Multiply it out.** `np.prod(x.shape) * x.itemsize` is the input's byte count. For (32, 256, 3) float32 that is 98,304 bytes. Inputs are rarely what exhausts memory, but the habit scales to activations, which are.

```python
import numpy as np
batch = np.zeros((32, 256, 3), dtype=np.float32)   # (batch, time, channel)
assert batch.shape[0] == 32 and batch.dtype == np.float32
print(batch.nbytes)                                 # 98304
```

What to inspect when a model misbehaves: `.shape` and `.dtype` at every boundary (after loading, after preprocessing, before the first layer). A shape can also be legal and wrong: an array of (256, 32, 3) passes a length check but has swapped time and batch. The shape states counts only; units, scaling and missing values are the preprocessing's contract, not the shape's.

beats.recap: A shape counts items per axis, batch first; multiply it out for bytes.

beats.title: A product runs only when the inner sizes agree
beats.outcome: Predict the shape a matrix product returns and read a core-dimension mismatch error to find the operand at fault.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-deep-learning-matmul-concept|matrix product]] pairs the last axis of the left operand with the first axis of the right one and sums along it, so those two sizes must match and then vanish. Notice the second state: a (32, 256, 3) batch times a (3, 8) weight keeps its leading axes and returns (32, 256, 8). The third state shows NumPy refusing a mismatch by naming both sizes. The last state is the dangerous one: square weights run either way round.
beats.hint: Write the two shapes one above the other and look at the touching numbers.

handbook.markdown:
Every dense layer is a matrix product plus a bias, so the product's contract is the first thing a network enforces. For `A @ B`, NumPy pairs A's last axis with B's second-to-last (for a 2-D weight, its first) and sums over it. Any extra leading axes on A are treated as a stack of matrices and carried through unchanged.

Run in this build with NumPy 2.5.3:

```python
import numpy as np
np.ones((32, 256, 3)) @ np.ones((3, 8))        # shape (32, 256, 8)
np.ones((32, 256, 3)) @ np.ones((2, 2))
# ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0,
# with gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?) (size 2 is different from 3)
```

How to read the error: *operand 1* is the right-hand array; *core dimension 0* is its first axis; the sizes in brackets are the two that disagree. The usual causes are a feature added or dropped upstream (the data now has 3 columns, the weights expect 2), a weight stored as (out, in) and used as (in, out), or a batch that lost its batch axis.

Why a legal product can be wrong: with a square (2, 2) weight, `X @ W1` and `X @ W1.T` both run, and only one is the network's arithmetic. Frameworks fix a convention (PyTorch's linear layer stores weights as (out_features, in_features) and multiplies by the transpose), but hand-written code must check one reading against a hand calculation. That is the demonstration to give: compute one row by hand, then show the batch reproduces it. The shape check proves the arithmetic can run, never that it is the intended arithmetic.

beats.recap: Inner sizes must match and vanish; a square weight can hide a transpose.

beats.title: A layer is a linear map followed by a bend
beats.outcome: Explain why a network needs a nonlinearity between linear layers, using the collapse of two linear maps into one.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-deep-learning-layer-concept|layer]] multiplies by a weight matrix, adds a bias, then applies an activation such as [[dbxfe-deep-learning-relu-concept|ReLU]], which turns negatives into zero. Notice the middle state: without the bend, the two layers fold into a single weight row, [4.0, 0.0], and a single bias, −3.5, so the extra layer added nothing. In the last state ReLU switches hidden unit one off for this reading; another reading may switch it on. That switching is what lets stacked layers draw bent decision boundaries.

samajh.text: Socho paint ki dukaan. Har shade do base colours ko apne ratio mein milata hai aur thoda white daalta hai; yeh ek hidden unit hai. Agar kisi shade ka hisaab 'minus do chammach' paint maange, dukaandaar bolta hai, bhai, negative paint nahi hota, aur us shade ko zero rakh deta hai. Phir final colour in shades ko apne ratio se milata hai. Agar dukaandaar negative ko zero na kare, toh do baar milana ek hi baar milane jaisa ho jaata hai.
samajh.mapping: The base colours are the inputs, each shade's recipe is a row of weights plus a bias, refusing a negative amount is ReLU, and the final mix is the output layer.
samajh.boundary: Real weights are learned from data rather than chosen by a shopkeeper, and values after the output layer can be negative; paint has no equivalent of the sigmoid that turns a score into a probability.

beats.hint: Multiply the two weight matrices together first and see what is left.

handbook.markdown:
The 3Blue1Brown lesson pictures each unit as holding a number and each layer as computing its numbers from the previous layer's; in arithmetic, a layer is `activation(W @ x + b)`. The weight matrix has one row per output unit and one column per input; the bias shifts each unit; the activation bends the result.

Why the bend is required: composition of linear maps is linear. With the worked weights, W2 @ W1 = [2.0·1.0 + 4.0·0.5, 2.0·(−2.0) + 4.0·1.0] = [4.0, 0.0], and W2 @ b1 + b2 = 2.0·0.5 + 4.0·(−1.0) − 0.5 = −3.5. So the two-layer network without ReLU is exactly the one-layer model 4.0·x1 − 3.5, which ignores temperature entirely. Stacking a hundred linear layers would still give one weighted sum.

ReLU, `max(z, 0)`, is the most common bend in hidden layers: cheap, and its slope is 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative ones. Its effect is membership: for each input, some units are on and some are off, and the network is a different linear map in each region of input space. That is how a network represents boundaries a single weighted sum cannot.

For a SQL-fluent reader: a layer is a projection (`SELECT w11*x1 + w12*x2 + b1 AS z1, …`) and ReLU is `GREATEST(z1, 0)`. Without the `GREATEST`, two projections compose into one projection.

What this beat does not claim: that ReLU is always the right activation (sigmoid, tanh and others exist and have tradeoffs), or that more layers are always better. A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every example never updates; that is a diagnostic for later beats.

beats.recap: No bend, no depth: two linear layers equal one; ReLU makes units switch per input.

beats.title: Two layers by hand turn 0.5 and 1.0 into a 62% defect score
beats.outcome: Compute a two-layer forward pass by hand for a new reading and check it against printed intermediate values.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-deep-learning-forward-concept|forward pass]] is the layers' arithmetic in order. Follow the equation states: layer 1 gives [−1.0, 0.25]; ReLU switches unit one off, leaving [0, 0.25]; layer 2 scores 4.0 × 0.25 − 0.5 = 0.5; the sigmoid turns 0.5 into 0.6225. Every value was reproduced by the lesson's NumPy code on CPU. Notice the batch table: the third reading switches both units off, so its probability, 0.3775, comes from the output bias alone.
beats.hint: Do layer 1 for both units before applying ReLU to either.

handbook.markdown:
The NumPy example in the lesson was run on CPU in this build (Python 3.12.3, NumPy 2.5.3). Its first printed line is the forward pass you can recompute by hand:

```text
z1 [-1.    0.25] h [0.   0.25] z2 [0.5] p [0.6225]
```

The weights are hand-chosen and untrained, so the 62% says nothing about real bearings; the point is that every number is traceable. The batch version is the same arithmetic on three rows at once:

```python
H = np.maximum(X @ W1.T + b1, 0.0)     # (3, 2) @ (2, 2) -> (3, 2)
P = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(H @ W2.T + b2))) # (3, 2) @ (2, 1) -> (3, 1)
```

which printed `P (3, 1) [0.6225 0.989 0.3775]`. Note the transposes: the weights are stored one row per output unit, so a batch with one row per reading multiplies by `W.T`.

How to demonstrate honestly: pick one reading, compute it by hand on a whiteboard, then show the code producing the same numbers, then change one weight and predict the direction of the change before running it. How to check your own code: the batch row for a reading must equal the single-reading result exactly; if not, a transpose or broadcast is wrong.

Limits of this example: two inputs and two hidden units hide the scale of real networks (millions of weights, many layers, convolution or attention instead of dense products), but not the mechanism. Real inputs also need the same preprocessing (standardization, the same feature order) at inference as in training, or the arithmetic is right and the answer is wrong. The sigmoid output is a model score, not a calibrated probability until checked against held-out labels.

beats.recap: Layer 1, ReLU, layer 2, sigmoid: 0.5 and 1.0 become 0.6225, and every step is checkable.

beats.title: The loss scores the guess; the gradient says which way each weight moves
beats.outcome: Compute a log loss and an output-layer gradient by hand and explain why a switched-off unit's weight receives no update.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-deep-learning-loss-concept|loss]] turns one prediction and its label into a number: −ln(0.6225) = 0.4741 for this real defect. Its gradient says how the loss changes as each weight moves. Follow the states: at the score the gradient is p − y = −0.3775; each output weight's gradient is that times the value it carried, so W2[0], fed by the switched-off unit, gets zero. [[dbxfe-deep-learning-gradient-concept|Gradient descent]] then steps W2[1] from 4.0 to 4.0094, and p rises to 0.6230.

samajh.text: Socho dhund wali raat mein pahaadi se neeche utarna hai. Neeche ki ghaati dikhti nahi, sirf pairon ke neeche ki dhalaan mehsoos hoti hai. Tum usi taraf chhota sa kadam rakhte ho jahan zameen sabse zyada neeche jaa rahi hai, phir ruk kar dobara mehsoos karte ho. Kadam bahut bada ho toh gaddhe ke paar nikal jaaoge; bahut chhota ho toh subah ho jaayegi.
samajh.mapping: Your height is the loss, the slope under your feet is the gradient, the length of each step is the learning rate, and each pause to feel the ground again is one batch.
samajh.boundary: A real loss surface has millions of directions at once, and each batch gives a slightly different slope; walking downhill can stop in a local hollow rather than the lowest valley.

beats.hint: A weight's gradient is the error multiplied by whatever flowed through that weight.

handbook.markdown:
3Blue1Brown's second chapter describes the cost as a measure of how badly the network does on its training examples and gradient descent as repeatedly stepping downhill on that cost. Here is one step, small enough to check.

**Loss.** For a yes/no label, log loss (binary cross-entropy) is −ln(p) when y = 1 and −ln(1 − p) when y = 0. Predicting 0.6225 for a real defect costs 0.4741; predicting 0.99 would cost 0.01; predicting 0.01 would cost 4.6. Confident mistakes are punished hardest.

**Gradient at the output.** With a sigmoid feeding log loss the derivative with respect to the score simplifies to p − y. Here −0.3775: raising z2 lowers the loss.

**Gradient for a weight.** By the chain rule, ∂loss/∂W2[j] = (p − y) × h[j]. The NumPy run printed `dW2 [[-0. -0.0944]]`. The `-0.` is a signed zero (−0.3775 × 0); it is simply zero. Unit one was off, so its outgoing weight gets no instruction from this reading.

**The step.** With learning rate 0.1, W2[1] becomes 4.0 − 0.1 × (−0.0944) ≈ 4.0094, and the recomputed p is 0.6230. That is one example; training averages the gradient over a batch and repeats for many steps.

```python
dW2 = (p - y)[:, None] * h[None, :]   # (1, 1) * (1, 2) -> (1, 2)
W2 = W2 - 0.1 * dW2
```

Backpropagation continues the chain rule into W1 and b1; libraries such as PyTorch's autograd do that bookkeeping. What to inspect when learning stalls: a loss that stops falling, gradients that are all near zero (units that are off for every example), or a learning rate so large that the loss jumps. A gradient is a local slope: it does not promise the best weights, only a better direction for this batch.

beats.recap: Loss −ln(0.6225) = 0.4741; gradient (p − y) × h; the off unit's weight does not move.

beats.title: An embedding is a learned row in a lookup table
beats.outcome: Explain how an embedding turns a category into a vector, how training changes it, and how to handle a category unseen in training.
beats.explanation: A supplier code cannot be multiplied, so an [[dbxfe-deep-learning-embedding-concept|embedding]] gives each code an index and each index a row of numbers the next layer multiplies. PyTorch documents nn.Embedding as a lookup table of fixed dictionary and size. Notice the second state: rows start random and move with the gradients like any weight, so S-0102 and S-0331, which predict alike, drift together. The last state shows why an unknown row is reserved before training: the table cannot grow at inference.
beats.hint: Think about what the table can and cannot do once its size is fixed.

handbook.markdown:
An embedding is the answer to "how do I feed a category to a network?" One-hot encoding a 40-supplier code gives 40 mostly-zero inputs and no notion that two suppliers are alike. An embedding table of shape (num_embeddings, embedding_dim), say (41, 3) with one reserved row, maps each code's index to a dense row, and those rows are weights: the backward pass updates the rows used in each batch.

```python
# NOT EXECUTED in this build (PyTorch is not installed here); shapes per the PyTorch reference.
import torch
table = torch.nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=41, embedding_dim=3)   # row 0 = unknown
idx = torch.tensor([2, 0])        # S-0331, then an unseen code mapped to 0
vectors = table(idx)              # shape (2, 3)
```

What the synthetic table shows: after training, rows for suppliers with similar defect behaviour sit close together, because similar rows produce similar downstream scores. Nobody hand-designs the numbers, and a single row means nothing on its own; distances between rows carry the meaning.

What fails: an index outside the table raises an error at inference. Reserve an index for unknown codes, map rare or unseen codes to it during training so it is learned, and keep the code-to-index mapping versioned with the model: a mapping rebuilt in a different order silently gives every supplier someone else's row.

The transfer: a language model's token embeddings are the same mechanism with a dictionary of tokens, and the vectors a retrieval index such as Databricks AI Search stores are embeddings of whole passages, computed by an embedding model. Limits: embeddings reflect the training data's patterns, including its biases, and a row for a category with few examples is noisy.

beats.recap: An id picks a row; gradients move the rows; reserve an unknown row before training.

beats.title: Training rewrites the weights; inference only reads them
beats.outcome: Distinguish a training step from an inference request and predict what changes, and what is held in memory, in each.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-deep-learning-training-concept|Training]] loops over labelled batches: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer update, and the weights change. Inference is one forward pass on a new input with frozen weights. Compare the two states: in the inference path the loss, backward pass and update are excluded, because there is no label and nothing to learn from. So scoring many clips teaches the model nothing, and serving needs far less memory than the training job did.
beats.hint: Ask what the model would need in order to learn from a prediction.

handbook.markdown:
Training is the only time weights change. One step: take a batch of inputs with labels, run the forward pass, compute the average loss, run the backward pass to get a gradient for every weight, and let the optimizer update the weights (and its own state, such as running averages). An epoch is one pass over the training data; a run is many epochs, checkpointed along the way. Databricks recommends Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning with MLflow tracking and autologging for model training, so each run's parameters, metrics and artifacts can be compared later.

Inference loads the trained weights once and runs forward passes on new inputs. There is no label, so no loss, no gradient and no update. In PyTorch this is written with the model in evaluation mode and gradient tracking off:

```python
# NOT EXECUTED in this build; PyTorch is not installed here.
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    p = torch.sigmoid(model(x))
```

Consequences worth explaining to a customer:

- A deployed model does not learn from traffic. Improvement requires collecting labels (here, inspection outcomes), running a new training job and deploying a new version.
- Memory differs: training holds weights, gradients, optimizer state and the batch's saved activations; inference holds the weights and one request's transient activations. A model that needed a GPU to train may serve comfortably on CPU.
- Preprocessing must be identical in both paths: the same standardization constants, feature order and embedding index mapping, versioned with the model.

What to inspect when production predictions look wrong: the preprocessing at serving versus training, the model version actually loaded, and whether the input distribution has shifted, before assuming the weights are at fault.

beats.recap: Training loops and rewrites weights with labels; inference runs one frozen forward pass.

beats.title: Memory grows with the batch; the model's fixed cost does not
beats.outcome: Split training memory into fixed and batch-proportional terms, find the largest batch that fits, and choose the first knob on out-of-memory.
beats.explanation: During a training step a GPU holds weights, gradients, optimizer state and every layer's activations for the whole batch. Only the last grows with [[dbxfe-deep-learning-batch-concept|batch size]]. Step through the synthetic tables: batch 128 fits in 848 MB, batch 512 needs 3,152 MB and fails. The last state is the first fix: [[dbxfe-deep-learning-accumulation-concept|gradient accumulation]] runs four batches of 64 before one update, behaving like batch 256 while holding only 464 MB of the [[dbxfe-deep-learning-memory-concept|GPU memory budget]].
beats.hint: Subtract the fixed cost from the budget before dividing by the per-window cost.

handbook.markdown:
A useful mental model of training memory, labelled as a model rather than a measurement:

**memory ≈ weights + gradients + optimizer state + batch × activations per example**

For 5 million float32 parameters, the weights take 5,000,000 × 4 bytes = 20 MB, the gradients another 20 MB, and an optimizer that keeps two values per weight (as Adam does) 40 MB: 80 MB fixed. Activations are what each layer saves for the backward pass; the 6 MB per window here is an assumption, and in a real network it depends on layer sizes and input length. Real frameworks also reserve workspace and cache memory, so measure the first run rather than trusting arithmetic.

Batch size trades three things: memory per step (linear in the batch), number of optimizer steps per epoch (64,000 windows at batch 64 is 1,000 steps, at 128 is 500), and the noise in each update. A bigger batch is not automatically better; the learning rate usually needs retuning and the validation curve decides.

On `CUDA out of memory`, in order:

1. Halve the batch, or keep the effective batch with gradient accumulation:

```python
# NOT EXECUTED in this build; PyTorch is not installed here.
for i, (X, y) in enumerate(loader):          # batches of 64
    loss = loss_fn(model(X), y) / 4          # scale so four add up to one mean
    loss.backward()                          # gradients accumulate
    if (i + 1) % 4 == 0:
        opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()          # one update per 256 examples
```

2. Mixed precision (`torch.amp`), which changes numerics and must be validated.
3. A larger GPU or, if even batch 1 does not fit, sharded training.

Adding data-parallel workers does not fix it: each worker still holds its own batch's activations. All figures here are synthetic; no GPU was used.

beats.recap: Fixed 80 MB plus 6 MB per window: shrink the batch or accumulate before anything else.

beats.title: Fine-tuning changes the weights; retrieval changes the input
beats.outcome: Choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning for a stated need and justify the choice by what each lever changes.
beats.explanation: "Make the model better" hides two different requests. [[dbxfe-deep-learning-finetune-concept|Fine-tuning]] continues training on your examples, so the weights change: format, tone and task habits move, but the model still cannot cite a source. [[dbxfe-deep-learning-retrieval-concept|Retrieval]] leaves the weights alone and puts relevant passages into the input at request time. Compare the two states: only retrieval produces a citation and updates when Monday's bulletin is re-indexed. The last state orders the levers by need.

samajh.text: Naye mechanic ko do tarah se taiyaar kar sakte ho. Ek: usse mahino tak practice karwao, haath baith jaata hai, aadatein badal jaati hain, par poocho 'yeh kahan likha hai' toh bata nahi paata. Do: bench pe company ka manual rakh do; har kaam se pehle sahi panna kholta hai aur page number bhi bata deta hai. Manual ka naya edition aaye toh sirf kitaab badlo, mechanic ko dobara sikhana nahi padta.
samajh.mapping: Months of practice are fine-tuning, which changes the weights; the manual on the bench is the retrieval index; opening the right page is the search; swapping in a new edition is re-indexing.
samajh.boundary: A model does not understand a passage the way a mechanic reads a manual; retrieval can open the wrong page, and fine-tuning can also teach some facts, only without citations and frozen at the training date.

beats.hint: Ask whether the need is a habit or a fact, and whether it changes weekly.

handbook.markdown:
Two levers, two different things changed.

**Fine-tuning** is training again, starting from existing weights, on examples of the behaviour you want. It is the right lever for a stable habit: an output format, a tone, a classification scheme, domain vocabulary the base model handles poorly. It costs GPU time, an evaluation set to prove the gain, and a new model version to serve and monitor. It is the wrong lever for facts that change: a bulletin learned into weights is stale next week and the answer cannot say where it came from.

**Retrieval** searches an index built from your documents when a request arrives and places the best passages in the model's input. Databricks AI Search (formerly Vector Search) is the platform's managed index: built from a Delta table of embedded text, queried for the most similar vectors, with hybrid keyword search. It is the right lever for changing facts that need citations; refreshing the index updates answers without retraining. It fails differently: the wrong passage wins, or the right one was never chunked well.

The order to try: a prompt with examples first (cheapest, fully reversible), then retrieval for knowledge, then fine-tuning for a behaviour gap that remains after measurement. Retrieval and fine-tuning can be combined.

Platform status matters here. Databricks documents its managed Foundation Model Fine-tuning feature as deprecated, with removal scheduled for 14 August 2026, and recommends AI Runtime, its serverless GPU environment, for training and fine-tuning. A fine-tuning plan therefore names your own training code on GPU compute and treats AI Runtime's preview status as a verification item. What to inspect before either lever: an evaluation set of real questions with expected answers, so the gain is measured, not asserted. The retrieval module goes deeper on index design.

beats.recap: Habits into weights by fine-tuning; changing facts into the input by retrieval; measure before either.

beats.title: Data parallelism splits the batch and shares the gradients
beats.outcome: Explain what data-parallel workers hold and exchange, and predict when adding workers helps speed but not memory.
beats.explanation: In [[dbxfe-deep-learning-parallel-concept|data parallelism]] every worker holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of the batch. Follow the states: each worker computes a gradient on its 128 windows; an all-reduce averages the gradients; both apply the identical update, so the copies never diverge. Notice the last state: every step moves a gradient as large as the model, which is why the documentation prefers one node with several GPUs and a single machine whenever it suffices.

handbook.markdown:
Data parallelism is the first way to use more than one GPU for training, and the one to reach for last.

**Mechanism.** PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel runs one process per model replica. Each process loads a different shard of every batch, runs forward and backward, and during the backward pass the replicas synchronize gradients so that when `backward()` returns, every replica holds the same averaged gradient. Each optimizer then applies the same update. The data is split, the gradients are shared, the weights never need to be sent.

**On Databricks.** Databricks Runtime ML includes TorchDistributor, a PySpark module that launches PyTorch training as Spark jobs and runs it across workers with `torch.distributed.run`; DeepSpeed and Ray are also included. Written, not executed here:

```python
# NOT EXECUTED in this build: needs a GPU cluster with Databricks Runtime ML.
from pyspark.ml.torch.distributor import TorchDistributor
TorchDistributor(num_processes=2, local_mode=False, use_gpu=True).run(train_fn)
```

Read the current TorchDistributor page for arguments before running anything.

**When it helps.** Throughput: two workers process twice the examples per step, minus the exchange cost. **When it does not.** Memory per GPU: each worker still holds the full model, its gradients, its optimizer state and its own local batch's activations. If one GPU runs out of memory at batch 64, four GPUs at batch 64 each run out too.

**Why the documentation says single machine first.** Databricks recommends training on a single machine when possible, because distributed code is more complex and slower due to communication overhead, and notes that one node with four GPUs is likely faster than four one-GPU workers. The synthetic 20 MB per step shows why: inside one node the exchange uses fast local links; across nodes it crosses the network every step. Measure step time on one node before distributing.

beats.recap: Full copies, split batch, averaged gradients every step; distribute only when one node is outgrown.

The ladder is original SpicyBrain guidance built on two documented recommendations: prefer a single machine, and prefer one node with several GPUs to several nodes with one.

**Rung 1, CPU smoke test (executed first).** A few hundred examples, the real preprocessing, the real model definition, one forward pass, one loss value and one optimizer step. In the table, the CNN's 83% recall beats the trees' 78%, but notice the second state: five more defects caught per hundred is worth adopting only if five times the cost of one missed defect exceeds the GPU hours and a second pipeline. handbook.markdown:
When is a simpler model, or no model, the better answer? More often than a GPU request suggests.

**Try the simplest thing that could meet the need.** A threshold rule has a physical meaning, no training pipeline and no drift monitoring. A classical model (logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees) on a few well-chosen features trains in minutes on CPU, is easier to explain, and is a strong baseline on tabular data. Neural networks tend to earn their cost on raw, high-dimensional signals such as audio, images and text, and at larger data scales; on small tabular data they often do not.

**Compare on the same evidence.** Same held-out period, same false-alarm rate, same labels. A network evaluated on a different week, or at a different threshold, has not been compared at all.

**Price the gain.** Five points of recall at 5% false alarms means five more defects caught per hundred defects. Multiply by the cost of a missed defect (scrap, rework, a returned assembly) and compare with the added cost: GPU hours to train and retrain, a second pipeline to maintain and monitor, and the time of whoever owns it. Pricing is a business input: if nobody can supply the cost of a miss, say so and do not pretend the decision is made.

**Keep the experiment honest.** Ship the baseline now so the plant benefits while the network is measured. Write a stop rule before the experiment, not after. Record a negative result as carefully as a positive one.

A non-ML answer is sometimes best of all: if most defects come from one worn tip, a maintenance schedule beats any detector. Ask what decision the model feeds before asking which model. All figures in this beat are synthetic.

beats.recap: Compare on the same held-out data, price the gain, ship the simpler model while the network earns its place.

extensionCards.prompt: What does automatic mixed precision change in a training step, and what must be re-checked afterwards?
extensionCards.answer: Some operations, such as linear layers and convolutions, run in float16 or bfloat16 while precision-sensitive ones such as reductions stay in float32; the loss curve and validation metric must be re-checked.
extensionCards.explanation: PyTorch's [[dbxfe-deep-learning-extension-amp-concept|automatic mixed precision]] (torch.amp) matches each operation to a type: lower precision where it is much faster, float32 where the range matters. Float16 training ordinarily pairs autocast with a gradient scaler so small gradients do not round to zero. A 16-bit value takes half the bytes of a float32, which is why it relieves activation memory, but the saving is workload-specific and the numerics change, so it comes after the batch-size knob and is judged on the validation curve, not on memory alone.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It names the second memory lever and why it is second: it changes numbers, not just bytes.

extensionCards.prompt: When the model itself no longer fits on one GPU, why does plain data parallelism not help, and what does the platform document instead?
extensionCards.answer: Data parallelism copies the whole model to every worker, so a model too large for one GPU is too large for each; the DeepSpeed distributor is documented for memory-limited models.
extensionCards.explanation: Data parallelism divides the batch, never the model: every worker holds full weights, gradients and optimizer state. When those alone exceed one GPU, the documented option on Databricks is the [[dbxfe-deep-learning-extension-deepspeed-concept|DeepSpeed distributor]], built on TorchDistributor and recommended for models that need more compute but are limited by memory; DeepSpeed offers optimized memory usage and pipeline parallelism. Sharding approaches such as PyTorch FSDP split those states across workers. None of this is needed until measurement shows the model does not fit.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It marks the boundary where data parallelism stops helping and names the documented next tool.

recap.title: One reading through the network, then the cost of doing it at scale
recap.markdown: **A shape is a contract; a layer is a linear map and a bend; a loss and its gradient say which way each weight moves; an embedding is a learned row.** Training holds weights, gradients, optimizer state and a batch of activations; inference holds weights and one request. Batch size is the first memory knob, gradient accumulation keeps the effective batch, and data parallelism shares gradients, never the model's memory burden. Fine-tuning changes weights; retrieval changes the input. On the platform, classic GPU compute, AI Runtime in preview and the distributors are climbed one rung at a time, every unrun step labelled, and only after a simpler model has fallen short. **Transfer challenge:** for a paint-line image model with batches of shape (32, 3, 224, 224), write the fixed and per-image memory terms, the first knob on out-of-memory, and the baseline it must beat.
